q: A wholesaler sells 1,000 LED bulbs to a hardware store, "F.O.B. Wholesaler's warehouse." The contract says nothing about when payment is due. The day the bulbs go to the carrier, the wholesaler demands payment and threatens to stop the shipment if not paid. Is the hardware store obligated to pay now?
o: Yes, because the risk of loss passed to the hardware store when the carrier took the bulbs.
Yes, because a seller who has shipped may always demand payment before the goods arrive.
Yes. In a shipment contract, delivery to the carrier is delivery to the buyer, so payment is due then.
No, because an F.O.B. term always requires the buyer to pay against the shipping documents.
No. Payment is due when and where the buyer is to receive the goods, even under a shipment term.
oe: When risk passes and when payment is due are separate questions. Risk passed; payment is not yet due.
There is no such rule. Unless the parties agreed otherwise, the buyer pays on receipt.
Section 2-310(a) separates the time of payment from the place of delivery. Payment waits for receipt.
That is the default only for F.O.B. vessel and F.A.S. (§ 2-319(4)). This is F.O.B. a warehouse.

Correct. Unless otherwise agreed, payment is due at the time and place at which the buyer is to receive the goods, even though the place of shipment is the place of delivery (§ 2-310(a)). The buyer may also inspect after arrival (§ 2-513(1)).
topic: Shipping terms · FOB shipment & destination (§ 2-319(1)(a), (b)) — FOB shipment; when payment is due

q: A con artist posing as a well-known art dealer buys a sculpture from its owner and pays with a check that clears, but the owner later learns the buyer lied about who he was. Before the owner acts, the con artist sells the sculpture to a collector who pays fair value and knows nothing of the fraud. The owner sues the collector to get it back. Who wins?
o: The collector, because the impostor had voidable title to pass on.
The owner, because a sale to an impostor is treated the same as a theft.
The owner, because a sale induced by fraud passes no title at all.
The owner, because the collector should have checked the seller's identity.
The collector, but only because the con artist's check cleared.
oe: Correct. A purchaser has voidable title, and can transfer good title to a good faith purchaser for value, even though the transferor was deceived as to the purchaser's identity (§ 2-403(1)(a)).
Section 2-403(1)(a) treats it as a purchase that passes voidable title.
Fraud makes the title voidable, not void. Only theft leaves the transferee with void title.
A GFP has no duty to investigate absent warning signs. Good faith is honesty in fact and fair dealing.
The check isn't what matters. Fraud as to identity still gives voidable title (§ 2-403(1)(a)).
topic: Shorthand · GFP & BIOCB (§ 2-403) — GFP: impostor gets voidable title

q: A restaurant orders 30 cases of wine shipped "C.O.D." When the carrier arrives, the restaurant asks to open the cases and check the vintages before paying. The driver refuses to hand anything over until the restaurant pays. Who is right?
o: The restaurant. A buyer always has the right to inspect before paying for goods.
Neither. They must split the difference by paying half before inspecting.
The restaurant, because the seller must allow inspection whenever it demands payment on delivery.
The driver. Under C.O.D., the buyer has no right to inspect before paying.
The driver, and by paying, the restaurant gives up any right to complain about the wine.
oe: That is only the default rule (§ 2-513(1)). C.O.D. is a contrary term that removes it.
Nothing in the Code provides for that. Under C.O.D. the buyer pays first.
Comment 2 to § 2-503 states that rule, but it carves out C.O.D. and similar terms.

Correct. When the contract provides for C.O.D. or similar terms, the buyer isn't entitled to inspect the goods before payment (§ 2-513(3)(a)). It can still inspect afterward and reject nonconforming goods.
Paying C.O.D. doesn't waive anything. Payment isn't acceptance (§ 2-512(2)).
topic: Shipping terms · COD & payment against documents (§§ 2-512, 2-513) — COD; buyer wants to look first

q: A homeowner signs a dealer's pre-printed sales form for a $9,000 generator. Buried in the form is a clause: "No modification is valid unless in a signed writing." The homeowner signs only at the bottom of the form. Later, the dealer's manager agrees by phone to an earlier delivery date. Can the dealer rely on the NOM clause to deny the change?
o: Yes, because the homeowner had a duty to read the form before signing it.
No, because a modification needs no consideration under Article 2.
No. A NOM clause on a merchant's form must be separately signed by a non-merchant.
Yes, because an oral modification is never valid under Article 2.
Yes. NOM clauses are enforceable between any parties to a sale of goods.
oe: The duty to read doesn't override the specific protection in § 2-209(2).
That is true (§ 2-209(1)), but it doesn't answer whether the NOM clause applies.
Correct. Under § 2-209(2), a NOM requirement on a form supplied by a merchant must be separately signed by the other party, unless that party is also a merchant. Signing the form once isn't enough.
Without an enforceable NOM clause, an oral modification can be valid (§ 2-209(1)), subject to the SOF in § 2-209(3).
They are enforceable, but § 2-209(2) adds a separate-signature requirement when a merchant's form binds a non-merchant.
topic: Shorthand · NOM & waiver (§ 2-209) — NOM on a merchant's form not separately signed

q: Brandywine Mills in Lancaster sells 300 bolts of denim to Harbor Outfitters in Wilmington, "F.O.B. Lancaster." Brandywine loads the denim onto a reputable carrier's truck, makes a reasonable shipping contract, and emails Harbor the tracking number. The truck crashes on I-95 and the denim is ruined. Must Harbor pay?
o: No. The carrier caused the loss, so only the carrier can be made to bear it.
Yes. Risk passed to Harbor when the denim was duly delivered to the carrier.
No. Under an F.O.B. term the seller keeps the risk until the goods reach the buyer.
Yes, but only because Harbor had already paid for the denim before it shipped.
No. Harbor never received the denim, and a merchant seller keeps the risk until receipt.
oe: The carrier may be liable to whoever has the risk, but as between seller and buyer the risk was already on Harbor.

Correct. F.O.B. the place of shipment is a shipment contract (§ 2-319(1)(a)). Brandywine met its § 2-504 duties, so risk passed on delivery to the carrier (§ 2-509(1)(a)). Harbor owes the price (§ 2-709(1)(a)) and can pursue the carrier.
That describes F.O.B. the place of destination. F.O.B. the seller's city puts the transit risk on the buyer.
Payment has nothing to do with when risk passes. The F.O.B. term and § 2-509(1)(a) decide it.
The receipt rule of § 2-509(3) applies only when the goods are not shipped by carrier or held by a bailee.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB shipment & destination (§ 2-319(1)(a), (b)) — FOB seller's city; truck crash

q: A steel fabricator building a storage tank on credit, with payment due on completion, becomes nervous about the owner's finances. It demands, as "adequate assurance," that the owner's president personally guarantee payment, put the full price into escrow, or give the fabricator an ownership share. The owner refuses, and the fabricator stops work. Who is in breach?
o: The owner, because it refused to give any assurance at all.
The owner, because a party with reasonable grounds for insecurity may demand any security it wants.
The owner, because a request for a letter of credit is always adequate assurance.
Neither, because both parties acted in good faith.
The fabricator, because its demands went far beyond adequate assurance.
oe: Refusing an improper demand isn't a repudiation. The demand has to be for adequate assurance.
Reasonable grounds let you demand adequate assurance, judged by commercial standards, not anything at all.
The fabricator didn't ask for an LOC here, and what is adequate depends on the facts.
Good faith doesn't save a demand that exceeds § 2-609. The fabricator's suspension was a breach.

Correct. Section 2-609 lets a party ask for adequate assurance of performance, not a better deal than it bargained for. Demanding guarantees, escrow, or equity rewrote the credit terms, so the fabricator's suspension was itself a breach (Pittsburgh-Des Moines Steel v. Brookhaven Manor).
topic: Shorthand · HTA, LOC & PDM (§ 2-609) — Demand that asks for too much

q: A buyer accepts a commercial oven, discovers a hidden defect that substantially impairs its value, and rightfully revokes its acceptance. While the buyer is waiting for the seller to pick it up, a fire at the buyer's restaurant destroys the oven, worth $30,000. The buyer's insurance pays $10,000. Who bears the remaining $20,000?
o: The buyer, because the oven was in the buyer's possession when it was destroyed.
The seller, to the extent the buyer's insurance falls short.
The buyer's insurer, which must pay the full $30,000.
The parties split it, because neither one caused the fire.
The buyer, because it had accepted the oven before the fire.
oe: Possession doesn't control here. Section 2-510(2) protects the revoking buyer.

Correct. When the buyer rightfully revokes acceptance, it may, to the extent of any deficiency in its effective insurance coverage, treat the risk of loss as having rested on the seller from the beginning (§ 2-510(2)).
The insurer pays what its policy covers. The seller bears the deficiency.
Article 2 doesn't split the loss. The seller bears the uninsured portion.
The buyer rightfully revoked that acceptance, which brings § 2-510(2) into play.
topic: Shipping terms · No term, presumptions & breach (§§ 2-503, 2-509, 2-510) — Revocation; buyer's insurance shortfall

q: A seller sells 300 marble slabs "ex-ship, Port of Wilmington." The ship arrives, the seller discharges the freight lien, and gives the buyer a delivery order the carrier must honor. While the ship's crane is swinging a pallet over the side, the pallet slips and the slabs shatter on the deck. Who bears the loss?
o: The buyer, because the ship had reached the port named in the contract.
The carrier alone, because the slabs were damaged by the carrier's own crane.
The buyer, because ex-ship is a shipment contract, so risk passed when the slabs were loaded abroad.
The seller, because ex-ship risk doesn't pass until the goods leave the ship's tackle.
None of the above.
oe: Arrival isn't enough. The slabs had to be unloaded.
The carrier may be liable to the seller. Between the parties, ex-ship puts the risk on the seller until unloading.
Ex-ship is the opposite: delivery from the ship at the arrival port, a destination-type term.

Correct. Under § 2-322(2)(b), risk passes to the buyer only when the goods leave the ship's tackle or are otherwise properly unloaded. These slabs never left the tackle. Ex-ship is a destination-type term.
One of the other choices is correct: The seller, because ex-ship risk doesn't pass until the goods leave the ship's tackle.
topic: Shipping terms · Ex-ship & no arrival, no sale (§§ 2-322, 2-324) — Ex-ship; damage during unloading

q: A seller delivers 200 office desks to a buyer's warehouse under a contract that says nothing about payment or inspection. The seller's driver demands a certified check before unloading and refuses to let the buyer open any boxes. The buyer refuses to pay. Who is in breach?
o: The buyer, because a seller may always insist on payment before the goods leave its truck.
The buyer, because tender of delivery and tender of payment are concurrent conditions.
Neither, because the contract is too indefinite without a payment term.
The seller, but only because it demanded a certified check rather than an ordinary check.
The seller, because absent agreement the buyer may inspect before paying or accepting.
oe: Only if the parties agreed to C.O.D. or similar terms. They didn't.
They are, but the buyer's duty to pay is subject to its right to inspect first.
Gap fillers supply the missing terms: payment on receipt (§ 2-310(a)) after inspection (§ 2-513(1)).
The form of payment isn't the problem. Refusing inspection is.

Correct. Unless otherwise agreed, the buyer has a right to inspect before payment or acceptance (§ 2-513(1)), and a seller who demands payment on delivery must first allow inspection (§ 2-503 cmt. 2). Refusing inspection impaired the seller's tender.
topic: Shipping terms · COD & payment against documents (§§ 2-512, 2-513) — Seller demands payment, refuses inspection

q: Keystone Steel in Pittsburgh sells beams to a builder in Wilmington, "F.O.B. Philadelphia rail yard." The beams are shipped by rail. A derailment destroys them about 50 miles outside Pittsburgh, before they reach Philadelphia. Who bears the loss?
o: Keystone, because F.O.B. a named point on the way is a destination contract as to that point.
The railroad alone, because it caused the derailment and the contract can't shift that loss.
The builder, because the beams were delivered to a rail carrier in Pittsburgh.
The builder, because only the buyer's own location can make an F.O.B. term a destination term.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Keystone had to get the beams to Philadelphia at its own expense and risk and tender them there (§ 2-319(1)(b)). The loss happened before that point, so the risk had not passed.
The railroad may be liable to the risk bearer, but between the parties the F.O.B. term allocates the risk.
That would be right for F.O.B. Pittsburgh. Naming Philadelphia moved the seller's responsibility to that point.
Any named place the seller must deliver to works. An intermediate point is a destination as to that point.
One of the other choices is correct: Keystone, because F.O.B. a named point on the way is a destination contract as to that point.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB shipment & destination (§ 2-319(1)(a), (b)) — FOB a point between seller and buyer

q: A Delaware importer buys 400 cases of olive oil from a Spanish exporter, "C.I.F. Port of Wilmington," and the parties agree the UCC governs. The exporter ships properly, buys the insurance, and tenders the bill of lading, insurance certificate, and invoice. The ship sinks. Must the importer pay?
o: Yes, but only for the freight and insurance portion of the price, not for the oil itself.
No. Under C.I.F. the seller's insurance protects the seller, so the seller bears the loss.
Yes. C.I.F. is a shipment contract, so the importer pays and claims on the insurance.
No. The importer never received the goods, so the exporter must ship replacements.
No. The exporter paid freight and insurance to Wilmington, which makes it a destination contract.
oe: The C.I.F. price is a lump sum (§ 2-320(1)). The importer owes all of it against the documents.
The insurance must provide for loss payable to the buyer's order (§ 2-320(2)(c)). It protects the buyer, who has the risk.

Correct. A C.I.F. contract is a shipment contract, with risk passing on shipment if the seller performed its obligations (§ 2-320 cmt. 1). The importer must pay against the documents (§ 2-320(4)) and is protected by the policy the seller bought for it.
The risk had passed on shipment. The exporter performed, so it has no duty to ship again.
That is the classic trap. Paying freight and insurance is built into the C.I.F. price and doesn't make it a destination contract.
topic: Shipping terms · CIF & C&F (§§ 2-320, 2-321) — CIF; ship sinks after proper shipment

q: A contract to supply custom display cases for a store opening says late delivery costs the seller $2,000 per day. At signing, that figure reasonably reflected the store's expected lost sales. The cases arrive five days late, but the store's opening was delayed anyway for an unrelated reason, so it lost almost nothing. Is the $10,000 enforceable?
o: No, because LD clauses are allowed only when actual damages are impossible to calculate.
Likely yes, because it was reasonable in light of the anticipated harm when the deal was made.
No, because an LD clause is valid only if it is conspicuous.
No, because liquidated damages can never exceed the harm actually suffered.
Yes, because courts enforce whatever liquidated amount the parties agree on.
oe: Difficulty of proof is one factor, not a requirement of impossibility.
Correct. Section 2-718(1) tests reasonableness in light of the anticipated or actual harm. The "or" means a clause reasonable at contracting can be enforced even if actual harm turned out smaller.
Nothing in § 2-718 requires an LD clause to be conspicuous.
The test is disjunctive: anticipated or actual harm. A reasonable forecast is enough.
Not whatever amount. An unreasonably large amount is void as a penalty (§ 2-718(1)).
topic: Shorthand · LD (§ 2-718) — LD: reasonable when made, actual harm smaller

q: Two lumber dealers agree by phone on a $40,000 sale. The seller emails a signed confirmation stating the quantity. The buyer reads it and says nothing for three weeks, then refuses to perform and denies any deal was made. What is the effect of the confirmation?
o: It removes the SOF defense; the seller must still prove the deal.
It satisfies the SOF against the buyer only up to $500.
It satisfies the SOF only if the buyer replied to the email, even to object.
It proves the contract, so the buyer is liable without any further evidence.
It has no effect, because the buyer never signed anything.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-201(2), a merchant's confirmation that isn't objected to in writing within 10 days satisfies the SOF against the recipient. Satisfying the SOF only removes the defense; the sender still has to prove the contract.
Nothing limits it to $500. It is enforceable up to the quantity stated.
A written objection within 10 days would defeat § 2-201(2). Silence is what makes it work.
The SOF is only a barrier to enforcement. Getting past it doesn't establish the contract.
That is the point of § 2-201(2): between merchants, the recipient's silence lets the sender's record bind it.
topic: Shorthand · SOF (§ 2-201) — SOF: merchant confirmation only opens the door

q: A "C.I.F. Port of Wilmington" contract adds: "Payment due on arrival of the goods." The seller ships properly and tenders the documents. The ship sinks in a storm and the goods never arrive. The buyer argues it never has to pay because the goods never arrived. Is the buyer right?
o: Yes. A buyer can't owe the price for goods that it never had a chance to inspect.
No, and the buyer must also pay interest from the date of shipment.
Yes, but the buyer must then refund the seller's insurance premium.
No. If the goods are lost, payment is due when they should have arrived.
Yes. A payment-on-arrival clause makes the contract a destination contract.
oe: Section 2-321(3) gives a preliminary inspection right only when the goods actually arrive. Lost goods don't change the payment duty.
Nothing in the Code adds interest here. The buyer pays when the goods should have arrived.
The buyer must pay, and the insurance policy is its protection.

Correct. Under § 2-321(3), when a C.I.F. contract provides for payment on or after arrival, payment is due on arrival, but if the goods are lost, delivery of the documents and payment are due when the goods should have arrived. The buyer still had the risk.
Section 2-321 says such clauses change the timing of payment, not the shipment character of C.I.F.
topic: Shipping terms · CIF & C&F (§§ 2-320, 2-321) — CIF; payment on arrival and goods lost

q: A lumber mill sells timber "F.A.S. vessel S.S. Chesapeake, Pier 4, Port of Wilmington." The mill delivers the timber alongside the vessel at Pier 4 in the usual way and obtains the receipt the carrier needs to issue a bill of lading. Before the ship's crew begins loading, a dock fire destroys the timber. Who bears the loss?
o: The port authority, because the fire started on its pier.
The mill, because it keeps the risk until the buyer receives a bill of lading.
The buyer, because the timber was properly delivered alongside.
The mill, because F.A.S. is a destination contract as to the port of shipment.
The mill, because the timber had not yet been loaded on board the vessel.
oe: The port's liability is separate. Between the parties, the F.A.S. term allocates the risk.
Section 2-319(2) requires the seller to obtain and tender a receipt for which the carrier must issue a bill of lading. The risk passed on delivery alongside.
Correct. Under § 2-319(2), the seller must at its own expense and risk deliver the goods alongside the vessel and obtain and tender a receipt. The seller did both, so the risk was on the buyer.
F.A.S. is a shipment-type term. The seller's job ends alongside the ship.
Loading is the F.O.B. vessel requirement. Under F.A.S. the seller never loads.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB vessel & FAS (§ 2-319(1)(c), (2) to (4)) — FAS; loss on the dock after delivery alongside

q: A bakery pays C.O.D. for a shipment of 50 bags of flour. When it opens the bags the next morning, it finds whole-wheat flour instead of the bread flour it ordered. The seller says the bakery accepted the flour by paying for it. Is the seller right?
o: Yes. By paying C.O.D. the buyer agrees to take the goods as they are.
Yes, because the bakery took the flour into its possession before inspecting it.
No. Paying before inspecting isn't acceptance.
No, but the bakery's only remedy is to keep the flour and sue for damages.
No, but only because the wrong flour was obvious without opening the bags.
oe: C.O.D. only removes inspection before payment. It doesn't make the buyer take nonconforming goods.
Taking possession isn't acceptance. The bakery has a reasonable time to inspect (§ 2-606(1)(b)).

Correct. Under § 2-512(2), payment required before inspection does not constitute an acceptance of goods or impair the buyer's right to inspect or any of its remedies. The bakery may reject within a reasonable time and recover what it paid.
The bakery isn't limited to damages. It hasn't accepted, so it may reject.
The bakery can reject either way. Payment isn't acceptance, whether the defect is obvious or not.
topic: Shipping terms · COD & payment against documents (§§ 2-512, 2-513) — COD paid; goods turn out wrong

q: A gasoline refiner sets the dealer tank wagon (DTW) price for its franchised dealers under an open-price contract. The price is within the range charged by other refiners and is applied equally to all dealers. Dealers prove the refiner secretly hoped the price would push some of them out so it could open company-operated retail stores (CORS). Under the majority view, is the price set in good faith?
o: No, because the refiner had a duty to disclose its plans for CORS to the dealers.
Yes. A reasonable price applied to all dealers alike is in good faith.
No. A seller can never set the price in an open-price contract with dealers.
Yes, because good faith under Article 2 means honesty in fact and nothing more.
No. Any improper motive makes a seller-set price a breach of § 2-305(2).
oe: Good faith isn't a duty of candor. No such disclosure duty exists.

Correct. The majority view (Shell Oil v. HRN; Autry Petroleum v. BP) treats a commercially reasonable, non-discriminatory posted price as within the safe harbor of § 2-305 cmt. 3. Mathis v. Exxon, which let subjective motive defeat good faith, is the minority view.
Section 2-305(2) expressly allows a price to be fixed by one party, so long as it is fixed in good faith.
Good faith also includes reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing (§ 1-201(b)(20)).
That is the Mathis (minority) approach. The question asks for the majority view.
topic: Shorthand · DTW & CORS (§ 2-305) — DTW: majority view on posted prices

q: A contract with an enforceable NOM clause calls for weekly deliveries every Monday. For two months the seller delivers on Wednesdays, and the buyer orally says that is fine. The buyer then sends written notice: "Starting in two weeks, deliveries must arrive on Mondays as the contract says." The seller has made no changes in reliance. Must the seller comply?
o: No. Once a buyer waives a term, the waiver binds it for the rest of the contract.
Yes, and the buyer may also recover damages for every late delivery in the past two months.
Yes. A waiver of future performance can be retracted by reasonable notice absent reliance.
No, because the buyer's oral approval violated the NOM clause and was itself a breach.
No. The two months of Wednesday deliveries permanently modified the contract.
oe: Section 2-209(5) lets the waiving party retract as to future performance.
The buyer waived those past deliveries. Retraction works only going forward.

Correct. The failed oral modification can operate as a waiver (§ 2-209(4)). A party who has waived an executory portion may retract by reasonable notification that strict performance will be required, unless retraction would be unjust because of a material change of position in reliance (§ 2-209(5)).
Agreeing to a change isn't a breach. The NOM clause only affects whether the change binds.
The NOM clause blocks an oral modification. The conduct can be a waiver, and waivers can be retracted.
topic: Shorthand · NOM & waiver (§ 2-209) — NOM: waiver and retraction

q: Buyer's signed purchase order says "Ship to Buyer, Dover" and lists a route and freight rate. Seller accepts by signed letter. A week later, Seller's invoice arrives reading "F.O.B. delivered." Seller loads the goods onto a carrier, and they are destroyed in transit. Buyer argues the invoice made it a destination contract. Is that likely to succeed?
o: Yes. "F.O.B. delivered" is an express agreement to deliver at the destination.
No, but only because neither party is a merchant, so § 2-207 can't apply.
Yes. "Ship to Buyer, Dover" already made it a destination contract, and the invoice confirms that.
Yes. Any ambiguity about the delivery term is resolved against the seller who drafted the invoice.
No. The contract was already formed, and a later invoice term doesn't change it on its own.
oe: The question is whether it became part of the contract. A unilateral term on a later invoice is at most a proposal for modification.
Merchant status isn't the reason. The contract was already formed, and the invoice term came too late.
"Ship to" language doesn't create a destination contract. The UCC presumes a shipment contract.
The contract wasn't ambiguous when formed. The invoice term came afterward.

Correct. The contract was formed by the order and the acceptance. "Ship to" only names where the goods are going, so the presumption of a shipment contract applies. See Problem 4-9: language added in a later invoice doesn't rewrite the deal.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB shipment & destination (§ 2-319(1)(a), (b)) — Later invoice says FOB delivered

q: A contract calls for delivery "F.A.S. vessel, Port of Newark." Unless otherwise agreed, the seller must do each of the following EXCEPT:
o: Obtain and tender a receipt for the goods for which the carrier must issue a bill of lading.
Load the goods on board the vessel at its own expense and risk.
Deliver the goods alongside the vessel in the manner usual in that port.
Deliver the goods on a dock that the buyer designates and provides, if the buyer does so.
Bear the expense and risk of getting the goods alongside the vessel.
oe: This is a seller duty under § 2-319(2)(b).
Correct. That is the F.O.B. vessel duty (§ 2-319(1)(c)). F.A.S. means free alongside: the seller's job ends with the goods next to the ship.
This is a seller duty under § 2-319(2)(a).
This is an alternative way to perform under § 2-319(2)(a).
The seller bears both under § 2-319(2) until the goods are alongside.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB vessel & FAS (§ 2-319(1)(c), (2) to (4)) — NOT a seller duty under FAS

q: Under a contract "F.O.B. Seller's warehouse," which of the following is NOT one of the seller's duties?
o: Obtain and promptly deliver any document the buyer needs to obtain possession.
Put the goods in the possession of a carrier at its own expense and risk.
Insure the goods for the buyer's benefit while they are in transit.
Make a contract for transportation that is reasonable given the nature of the goods.
Promptly notify the buyer that the goods have been shipped.
oe: This is a duty under § 2-504(b).
This is a duty. F.O.B. the place of shipment requires it (§ 2-319(1)(a); § 2-504(a)).
Correct. Section 2-504 does not require the seller to insure. That is one reason the seller must notify the buyer of shipment: so the buyer, who bears the transit risk, can insure.
This is a duty under § 2-504(a). Improper packaging or the wrong kind of carrier can violate it.
This is a duty under § 2-504(c), although missing it matters only if material delay or loss results.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB shipment & destination (§ 2-319(1)(a), (b)) — NOT a seller duty under FOB shipment

q: Seller claims Buyer orally agreed to buy a $3,000 hot tub. Which of the following would NOT take the claim outside the SOF as against Buyer?
o: Seller's signed confirmation mailed to Buyer, a consumer, who never objects.
Seller's substantial start on a custom hot tub not suitable for sale to others.
Buyer's admission in a deposition that she agreed to buy the hot tub.
Buyer's receipt and acceptance of the hot tub before refusing to pay.
Buyer's signed email saying, "Confirming my order of one Model 7 hot tub."
oe: Correct. The merchant-confirmation rule of § 2-201(2) works only "between merchants." A consumer's silence doesn't let the seller's record bind the consumer.
Specially manufactured goods satisfy § 2-201(3)(a) if the seller began before notice of repudiation.
An admission in pleading, testimony, or otherwise in court satisfies § 2-201(3)(b).
Goods received and accepted satisfy § 2-201(3)(c).
A signed record by the party to be charged that indicates a contract and states a quantity satisfies § 2-201(1).
topic: Shorthand · SOF (§ 2-201) — SOF: what does NOT satisfy it against the buyer

q: A buyer agrees to buy equipment for $20,000 and pays a $3,000 deposit. The contract has no liquidated damages clause. The buyer then wrongfully refuses to take the equipment, and the seller resells it at the same price with no proven damages. How much of the deposit must the seller return?
o: $3,000. The seller suffered no damages, so it must return the full deposit.
$1,500. The seller keeps half the deposit as a reasonable forfeiture.
Nothing, because 20% of the price ($4,000) is more than the deposit.
$2,500. The seller keeps the lesser of 20% of the price or $500.
None of the above.
oe: The statute lets the seller keep up to $500 here even without proving damages.
Nothing in § 2-718 provides for keeping half. The formula is 20% or $500, whichever is less.
The seller keeps the smaller of the two figures, which is $500, not $4,000.

Correct. Absent an LD term, a breaching buyer gets back what it paid beyond 20% of the value of its total performance or $500, whichever is smaller (§ 2-718(2)(b)). 20% of $20,000 is $4,000, so the seller keeps $500 and returns $2,500, subject to any proven damages (§ 2-718(3)).
One of the other choices is correct: $2,500. The seller keeps the lesser of 20% of the price or $500.
topic: Shorthand · LD (§ 2-718) — LD: restitution to a breaching buyer

q: Same parties, but the contract says "F.O.B. Harbor Outfitters, Wilmington." Brandywine hands the denim to a reputable carrier, and the truck crashes halfway to Wilmington. What is the result?
o: Brandywine bears the loss, but only if Brandywine also agreed in writing to pay the freight.
Harbor bears the loss, because risk passes when the goods are delivered to any carrier.
The loss is split between the parties, because neither one caused the crash.
Harbor bears the loss, because the UCC presumes every shipping contract is a shipment contract.
Brandywine bears the loss, because it had to get the denim to Wilmington and tender it there.
oe: The F.O.B. destination term alone puts the risk on Brandywine. Who pays freight doesn't decide the risk question.
That is the shipment-contract rule. Naming the buyer's location after F.O.B. makes it a destination contract.
Article 2 doesn't split losses. One party bears the risk, and here it is the seller.
The presumption applies only when the contract doesn't expressly require delivery at a destination. "F.O.B. Harbor, Wilmington" does.

Correct. F.O.B. the place of destination is a destination contract: the seller must transport the goods there at its own expense and risk and tender them (§ 2-319(1)(b)). Risk passes only on due tender at the destination (§ 2-509(1)(b)).
topic: Shipping terms · FOB shipment & destination (§ 2-319(1)(a), (b)) — FOB buyer's city; loss in transit

q: A seller agrees to ship 600 laptops "C.I.F. Port of Newark." The seller puts the laptops on a ship and sends the bill of lading and invoice, but to save money it never buys the insurance. The ship sinks. Who bears the loss?
o: The buyer, but it may deduct the cost of the missing insurance from the price.
The buyer, because C.I.F. is a shipment contract and the laptops were delivered to the carrier.
The buyer, because it could have bought its own insurance once it learned of the shipment.
The seller, but only if the buyer rejected the documents before the ship sank.
The seller, because it never did everything C.I.F. required, so the risk never passed.
oe: A price deduction doesn't cure the buyer's loss of protection. The seller bears the risk.
Shipment passes risk only if the seller fully performed. Skipping the insurance is a failure to perform.
Under C.I.F. the insurance is the seller's job, and the buyer is entitled to rely on it.
The tender of documents was defective whether or not the buyer had acted yet.

Correct. Under C.I.F. the seller must obtain the insurance (§ 2-320(2)(c)), and risk passes on shipment only if the seller has properly performed all its obligations (§ 2-320 cmt. 1). Without the policy, the tender was defective.
topic: Shipping terms · CIF & C&F (§§ 2-320, 2-321) — CIF; seller skips the insurance

q: A furniture dealer sells a dining set to a customer and agrees to deliver it in the dealer's own truck. The contract has no shipping term. On the way to the customer's house, the dealer's truck is hit by a drunk driver and the set is destroyed. Who bears the loss?
o: The customer, because the UCC presumes a shipment contract when the contract is silent.
The dealer, but only because the contract required delivery to the customer's house.
The customer, because risk passes when the goods are loaded onto any delivery vehicle.
The dealer, because a merchant seller keeps the risk until receipt.
The drunk driver alone, so neither party bears the loss under the contract.
oe: The presumption applies to shipment by carrier. This was direct delivery by the seller.
The result rests on § 2-509(3), not on a destination term. The dealer is a merchant who never delivered.
Section 2-509(1) is about delivery to a carrier, meaning an independent one. The seller's own truck doesn't count.
Correct. A seller delivering in its own truck isn't shipping by carrier, so § 2-509(1) doesn't apply. Under § 2-509(3), a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods.
The tortfeasor may be liable, but between seller and buyer, § 2-509(3) puts the risk on the dealer.
topic: Shipping terms · No term, presumptions & breach (§§ 2-503, 2-509, 2-510) — Seller's own truck is not a carrier

q: A thief steals a road bike from a garage and sells it on an online marketplace to a buyer who pays a fair price and has no reason to suspect anything. The original owner finds the bike and demands it back. Who wins?
o: The owner, because a thief has void title and can't pass good title to anyone.
The buyer, because she bought in the ordinary course of business.
The buyer, but she must be repaid her purchase price by the owner.
The owner, but only if he reported the theft before the sale.
The buyer, because she was a good faith purchaser for value.
oe: Correct. A thief gets no title, so nobody downstream, however innocent, gets title either. Section 2-403(1) protects good faith purchasers only from a transferor with voidable title.
The thief wasn't a merchant entrusted with the bike, so entrustment under § 2-403(2) doesn't apply.
The owner owes the buyer nothing. Her claim is against the thief, for breach of the title warranty (§ 2-312).
Reporting is irrelevant. Void title can't be cured by an innocent purchase.
GFP status protects a buyer only when the seller had voidable title. A thief has void title.
topic: Shorthand · GFP & BIOCB (§ 2-403) — GFP: thief passes nothing

q: A student is trying to keep the ocean shipping terms straight. Which statement correctly pairs F.A.S. and ex-ship?
o: F.A.S. is a shipment-type term; ex-ship is a destination-type term.
Both are shipment contracts, because both involve ocean carriers.
F.A.S. and ex-ship both require the buyer to pay against documents.
F.A.S. requires the seller to load the goods; ex-ship requires the buyer to unload them.
Both are destination contracts, because both name a port.
oe: Correct. F.A.S. is a shipment-type term: the seller delivers alongside the vessel (§ 2-319(2)). Ex-ship is a destination-type term: risk passes when the goods leave the ship's tackle at the named port (§ 2-322(2)(b)).
Ex-ship keeps the risk on the seller through the voyage, so it isn't a shipment-type term.
Payment against documents is the default for F.A.S. (§ 2-319(4)), not for ex-ship.
F.A.S. doesn't require loading (that is F.O.B. vessel). Ex-ship requires the goods to be properly unloaded before risk passes.
Naming a port doesn't decide it. F.A.S. names the departure port; ex-ship names the arrival port.
topic: Shipping terms · Ex-ship & no arrival, no sale (§§ 2-322, 2-324) — Classify FAS and ex-ship

q: A seller sells 1,000 bushels of wheat "C.I.F. Port of Newark" and the contract adds: "Seller warrants the wheat will arrive at not less than 98% of shipped weight." Normal drying shrinks the wheat to 96% of its weight in transit. Which statement is correct?
o: The buyer bears the shrinkage, because C.I.F. puts all transit risk on the buyer.
The seller bears that ordinary shrinkage, but the deal is still a shipment contract.
The seller bears the shrinkage only if it was caused by the carrier's negligence.
The warranty is void, because a C.I.F. seller can't make promises about arrival condition.
The warranty converts the C.I.F. contract into a destination contract for all purposes.
oe: The arrival warranty is a contrary agreement that shifts ordinary shrinkage to the seller.

Correct. Under § 2-321(2), an agreement about quality or condition on arrival puts the risk of ordinary deterioration, shrinkage, and the like in transit on the seller, but it doesn't affect when risk of loss otherwise passes or make the deal a destination contract.
Ordinary shrinkage is shifted to the seller regardless of fault. That is what the warranty covers.
Section 2-321(2) expressly contemplates such terms.
Section 2-321(2) says it does not. Only the ordinary transit deterioration shifts to the seller.
topic: Shipping terms · CIF & C&F (§§ 2-320, 2-321) — CIF; warranty of condition on arrival

q: A contract to sell a printing press "F.O.B. Seller's plant" also says: "Notwithstanding any other term, Seller bears all risk of loss until the press is installed and running at Buyer's shop." The press is destroyed in a carrier's accident on the way. Who bears the loss?
o: The carrier, because the accident occurred during transit.
The buyer, because a risk clause is unenforceable unless it is conspicuous.
The buyer, because the specific F.O.B. term controls over the general risk clause.
The seller, because the parties may agree to a different allocation of the risk.
The buyer, because the F.O.B. term is a statutory delivery term the parties can't vary.
oe: The carrier's liability is separate. Between the parties, their own agreement allocates the risk.
No conspicuousness requirement applies to a risk-allocation term.
The risk clause is itself specific and says "notwithstanding any other term." It controls.
Correct. The risk-of-loss rules apply subject to contrary agreement (§ 2-509(4)). The parties' express allocation overrides the default F.O.B. shipment rule.
The F.O.B. definitions apply unless otherwise agreed (§ 2-319(1)). The parties agreed otherwise.
topic: Shipping terms · No term, presumptions & breach (§§ 2-503, 2-509, 2-510) — Contrary agreement controls

q: An owner leaves her vintage guitar with a shop for repairs. The shop only repairs instruments; it has never sold instruments. The shop's owner sells the guitar to a customer who pays fair value and believes the shop owns it. Can the customer keep the guitar?
o: Yes, but the owner may recover the guitar if she pays the customer's price.
Yes. The customer bought in good faith and paid value, which is all a BIOCB needs.
No, because entrustment never applies when goods are left for repair.
Yes. Any delivery of goods to a merchant is an entrustment that protects good faith buyers.
No. Entrustment protects a BIOCB only if the merchant deals in goods of that kind.
oe: There is no buy-back rule. Either the customer took good title or he didn't.
A BIOCB must also buy in the ordinary course from someone in the business of selling goods of that kind.
Leaving goods for repair can be an entrustment, as in the jeweler example. It fails here only because this shop doesn't sell guitars.
The merchant must deal in goods of that kind. A repair-only shop doesn't.

Correct. Under § 2-403(2), entrusting goods to a merchant who deals in goods of that kind gives the merchant power to transfer the entruster's rights to a buyer in ordinary course. A repair-only shop doesn't sell guitars, and a BIOCB must buy from a person in the business of selling goods of that kind (§ 1-201(b)(9)).
topic: Shorthand · GFP & BIOCB (§ 2-403) — BIOCB: shop that only repairs

q: A buyer agrees to pay against documents for 100 glass-front display cases. When the cases arrive and the carrier opens the trailer, before any inspection, every case can be seen with its glass shattered. The documents are presented the same day. Must the buyer pay?
o: No. Nonconformity that appears without inspection excuses payment even under a pay-first term.
Yes, and it must then sue for a refund once it formally inspects the cases.
No, because a buyer may always refuse to pay until it accepts the goods.
Yes, unless the buyer can prove the seller knew the glass was broken.
Yes. A buyer who agreed to pay against documents must pay no matter what happened to the goods.
oe: Correct. Where the contract requires payment before inspection, nonconformity doesn't excuse payment unless it appears without inspection (§ 2-512(1)(a)), or fraud would justify an injunction under § 5-109(b). Shattered glass in plain view qualifies.
That is the general rule, but obvious nonconformity is the exception.
Not under a pay-first term. The buyer is excused here only because the damage is obvious.
The seller's knowledge isn't required. The § 2-512(1)(a) exception turns on what is apparent without inspection.
Section 2-512(1)(a) is an exception for nonconformity that appears without inspection.
topic: Shipping terms · COD & payment against documents (§§ 2-512, 2-513) — Payment before inspection; obvious defect

q: A buyer contracts for 10,000 bags of rice "F.O.B. vessel M/V Patriot, Port of Baltimore." The rice is loaded and the seller tenders the bill of lading and invoice. The buyer refuses to pay until the ship reaches its home port and it can inspect the rice. The contract says nothing else about payment. Is the buyer within its rights?
o: Yes. Payment is due when and where the buyer receives the goods, which is at its home port.
No. Unless otherwise agreed, an F.O.B. vessel buyer must pay against the required documents.
Yes. A buyer always has the right to inspect goods before paying for them.
No, because the risk passed when the rice was loaded, and payment is always due when risk passes.
Yes, because a seller may not demand payment until the buyer has accepted the goods.
oe: Section 2-319(4) supplies a different rule for F.O.B. vessel: payment against documents.

Correct. Under F.O.B. vessel or F.A.S., unless otherwise agreed, the buyer must make payment against tender of the required documents (§ 2-319(4)), and payment against documents waives inspection before payment (§ 2-513(3)(b)).
That is only the default rule. F.O.B. vessel and documentary terms displace it (§ 2-513(3)).
Risk and payment are separate questions. The documents rule of § 2-319(4) is what requires payment.
Payment is not acceptance (§ 2-512(2)), and the buyer can still inspect and reject after it pays.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB vessel & FAS (§ 2-319(1)(c), (2) to (4)) — FOB vessel; pay against documents

q: A buyer buys a commercial boiler, delivered and installed in March 2020. It carries the ordinary implied warranty of merchantability and no express warranty about future performance. A latent defect causes it to fail in June 2025, and the buyer sues in July 2025. Is the warranty claim timely?
o: Yes. The period runs from when the buyer discovered or should have discovered the defect.
Yes. Article 2's statute of limitations is six years for commercial buyers.
Yes. The period runs from when the boiler actually failed in June 2025.
No. The claim accrued on tender in March 2020, so the four-year period ran in 2024.
No, because warranty claims must be brought within one year after delivery.
oe: The discovery rule applies only when a warranty explicitly extends to future performance. This one doesn't.
The Article 2 period is four years (§ 2-725(1)).
A failure date matters only for a warranty that explicitly extends to future performance.
Correct. A breach of warranty occurs when tender of delivery is made, regardless of the buyer's lack of knowledge (§ 2-725(2)). The four-year period (§ 2-725(1)) expired in March 2024.
One year is the shortest period the parties may agree to. The default is four years.
topic: Shorthand · SOL (§ 2-725) — SOL: warranty breach accrues on tender

q: A seller stores 500 bales of cotton at an independent warehouse. To sell them, the seller hands the buyer a nonnegotiable warehouse receipt at 9 a.m. At 10 a.m., before the buyer has had any chance to present it to the warehouse, a fire destroys the bales. Who bears the loss?
o: The buyer, because risk passes as soon as the buyer receives any document of title.
The warehouse, because a bailee bears the risk of loss of the goods it stores.
The buyer, because goods held by a bailee are at the buyer's risk once the contract is made.
The seller, because the buyer hadn't had a reasonable time to present the document.
None of the above.
oe: That is the rule for a negotiable document (§ 2-509(2)(a)). A nonnegotiable receipt requires a reasonable time to present it.
The warehouse is liable only for its own failure of care. Between the parties, the seller had the risk.
Section 2-509(2) sets specific triggers. Making the contract isn't one of them.

Correct. When the buyer receives a nonnegotiable document, risk passes only after the buyer has had a reasonable time to present it to the bailee (§ 2-509(2)(c); § 2-503(4)(b)). One hour isn't a reasonable time.
One of the other choices is correct: The seller, because the buyer hadn't had a reasonable time to present the document.
topic: Shipping terms · No term, presumptions & breach (§§ 2-503, 2-509, 2-510) — Bailee; nonnegotiable document

q: A supply contract is silent on shortfalls. In the parties' ten earlier contracts, the buyer always accepted shipments up to 3% short without complaint. Industry practice allows shipments up to 8% short. This time the seller ships 6% short. Which controls?
o: The course of dealing, so the 6% shortfall falls outside what the parties have accepted.
The course of dealing, but only if the seller is a merchant.
Neither, because evidence outside the contract can't be used when the contract is silent.
The usage of trade, because industry-wide practice outweighs one pair of parties' habits.
The usage of trade, because course of dealing only counts if it was put in writing.
oe: Correct. When course of dealing and usage of trade can't be read consistently, course of dealing prevails over usage of trade (§ 1-303(e)). The hierarchy is express terms, then CoP, then CoD, then UoT.
The § 1-303 hierarchy doesn't depend on merchant status.
Silence is exactly when CoD and UoT supply meaning (§ 1-303(d)).
The hierarchy runs the other way. The parties' own history is better evidence of their meaning.
Course of dealing is conduct. No writing is needed.
topic: Shorthand · CoP, CoD & UoT (§ 1-303) — CoD beats UoT

q: A buyer orders 50 tons of coffee beans "C. & F. Port of Wilmington." The seller ships properly, pays the freight, and tenders the bill of lading and invoice. The ship sinks. The buyer never bought insurance and argues that the seller should have. Who bears the loss?
o: The loss is split, because neither party insured the coffee.
The buyer, but only if the contract expressly stated that the buyer had to insure.
The buyer, because C. & F. is a shipment contract and the seller has no duty to insure.
The seller, because a seller who pays the freight to the destination bears the transit risk.
None of the above.
oe: Article 2 doesn't split the loss. The buyer had the risk.
No express term is needed. The definition of C. & F. leaves insurance to the buyer.

Correct. C. & F. means cost and freight: the same as C.I.F. except for the insurance obligation (§ 2-320(3)). It is a shipment contract, so the buyer bore the risk once the seller shipped properly, and insuring was the buyer's job.
Paying freight doesn't make a destination contract. C. & F. is a shipment term.
One of the other choices is correct: The buyer, because C. & F. is a shipment contract and the seller has no duty to insure.
topic: Shipping terms · CIF & C&F (§§ 2-320, 2-321) — C&F; uninsured buyer

q: A café orders 40 espresso grinders, model G-200, "F.O.B. Seller's dock." Seller ships 40 of the older G-100 model by mistake, properly packed, and notifies the café. The truck is hit by a falling tree and the grinders are destroyed. Who bears the loss?
o: Seller, but only for the difference in value between the G-100 and the G-200.
The café, because F.O.B. Seller's dock passes the risk when the goods reach the carrier.
The café, unless it rejected the grinders before the truck was hit.
The café, because the tree, not the wrong model, caused the loss.
Seller, because the tender was nonconforming, so the risk never shifted to the café.
oe: The risk of loss is all or nothing. Seller bears the whole loss.
That rule applies to a conforming shipment. Section 2-510(1) overrides § 2-509 when the seller is in breach.
The café couldn't reject goods it never saw, and it didn't need to. The risk stayed with Seller under § 2-510(1).
Section 2-510(1) doesn't require the nonconformity to cause the loss. A nonconforming tender keeps the risk on the seller.

Correct. When a tender or delivery so fails to conform as to give a right of rejection, the risk stays on the seller until cure or acceptance (§ 2-510(1)). Shipping the wrong model is that kind of failure.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB shipment & destination (§ 2-319(1)(a), (b)) — Nonconforming goods shipped FOB seller

q: A seller agrees to sell a cargo of sugar "no arrival, no sale." It ships conforming sugar on a seaworthy vessel, which sinks in a hurricane through no fault of the seller. The buyer sues for damages for nondelivery. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer must pay the price, because the risk passed to it when the sugar was shipped.
The buyer wins, but only the difference between the market price and the contract price.
The buyer loses, because the contract is avoided.
The buyer loses, but only if the seller offers substitute sugar within a reasonable time.
The buyer wins, because a seller under a destination-type term guarantees arrival.
oe: Under this term the seller loses the sale. The buyer doesn't pay for sugar that never arrived.
There is no breach, so there are no damages.

Correct. Under § 2-324, the seller must properly ship conforming goods but assumes no obligation that they will arrive unless it caused the non-arrival. When the goods are lost entirely, the contract is avoided (§ 2-324(b); § 2-613).
The seller has no duty to substitute. The contract is simply avoided.
That is exactly what "no arrival, no sale" takes away. The seller bears the loss of the goods but not liability for non-arrival.
topic: Shipping terms · Ex-ship & no arrival, no sale (§§ 2-322, 2-324) — No arrival, no sale; total loss

q: In Mathis v. Exxon, the dealers persuaded a jury that Exxon set the DTW price in bad faith. Which of the following was NOT part of the evidence the dealers relied on?
o: Exxon admitted in writing that it set the price to bankrupt the dealers.
A number of the franchisees were unprofitable at the DTW price.
Exxon stopped the franchisees from buying gas from jobbers.
Exxon planned to replace a number of its franchises with company-operated retail stores.
The DTW price was higher than the rack price plus the cost of transportation.
oe: Correct. There was no such admission. The dealers relied on circumstantial evidence of motive, which is why the case matters: subjective intent was enough even though the price itself was in the market range.
This was part of the evidence (W3-S45).
This was part of the evidence (W3-S45).
This was part of the evidence (W3-S45).
This was part of the evidence (W3-S45).
topic: Shorthand · DTW & CORS (§ 2-305) — Mathis evidence of bad faith

q: Under a "C.I.F. Port of Wilmington" contract, unless otherwise agreed, the seller must do each of the following EXCEPT:
o: Put the goods in the carrier's possession and get a negotiable bill of lading to Wilmington.
Load the goods and obtain a receipt showing that the freight has been paid.
Tender the goods to the buyer at the Port of Wilmington.
Forward and tender all the documents with commercial promptness.
Obtain insurance on the goods, including war risk where obtainable, payable to the buyer's order.
oe: This is a seller duty under § 2-320(2)(a).
This is a seller duty under § 2-320(2)(b).
Correct. A C.I.F. seller tenders documents, not goods at the destination. C.I.F. is a shipment contract, and the buyer can't demand delivery of the goods in place of the documents (§ 2-320(4)).
This is a seller duty under § 2-320(2)(e).
This is a seller duty under § 2-320(2)(c).
topic: Shipping terms · CIF & C&F (§§ 2-320, 2-321) — NOT a CIF seller duty

q: A seller and buyer are drafting a contract for goods to be shipped by carrier from the seller's plant in Dover to the buyer's factory in Newark. Which of the following terms would make it a destination contract?
o: "Deliver to Buyer's factory, Attention: Receiving Dept."
"F.O.B. Buyer's factory, Newark."
"Freight prepaid by Seller to Buyer's factory."
"Seller will arrange shipment by a carrier of Seller's choice."
"Ship to Buyer's factory, Newark."
oe: In Windows v. Jordan Panel, "delivered to" a site only named where the goods were going. It stayed a shipment contract.
Correct. F.O.B. the place of destination requires the seller to transport the goods there at its own expense and risk and tender them there (§ 2-319(1)(b)).
A seller's duty to pay freight doesn't by itself make a destination contract (§ 2-503 cmt. 5).
This only says the seller picks the carrier, which it does in any shipment contract (§ 2-504(a)).
"Ship to" just names where the goods are going. The shipment presumption still applies.
topic: Shipping terms · No term, presumptions & breach (§§ 2-503, 2-509, 2-510) — Which phrase makes a destination contract

q: A grain dealer sells 2,000 tons of soybeans "F.O.B. vessel M/V Delmarva, Port of Wilmington." While the dealer's stevedores are lifting the last load into the hold, a crane cable snaps and that load falls into the river. Who bears the loss of that load?
o: The loss is split, because the crane accident was no one's fault.
The buyer, because the goods had been delivered to the port named in the contract.
The buyer, because F.O.B. vessel is a shipment contract, so the risk is the buyer's at the dock.
The dealer, because under F.O.B. vessel the seller must load the goods on board at its own risk.
The ship's owner, because cargo at the side of a ship is always the vessel's responsibility.
oe: Article 2 doesn't split the loss. The term puts loading risk on the seller.
Reaching the port isn't enough under F.O.B. vessel. The seller must also load the goods on board.
F.O.B. vessel extends the seller's risk through loading. Risk passes once the goods are on board.
Correct. Under § 2-319(1)(c), the seller must "at his own expense and risk load the goods on board." Goods that never made it on board were still at the seller's risk.
The vessel's liability is separate. Between seller and buyer, the F.O.B. vessel term allocates the risk.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB vessel & FAS (§ 2-319(1)(c), (2) to (4)) — FOB vessel; loss during loading

q: A signed contract for a delivery van has a clause stating: "This writing is the complete and exclusive statement of the parties' agreement." The buyer wants to prove that before signing, the seller orally promised to install a roof rack at no charge. The written contract says nothing about a roof rack. Is the evidence admissible?
o: Yes, because the parol evidence rule never applies to transactions with a consumer.
Yes. The roof rack doesn't contradict anything in the writing, so it may come in.
No, but only because the van costs more than $500 and the SOF applies.
Yes. The PER doesn't apply to oral promises, only to prior written ones.
No, because the writing is complete and exclusive.
oe: The PER applies to all sales under Article 2. Consumer status doesn't take it away.
That is the rule for a writing that is final but not complete and exclusive. This one is complete and exclusive.
This is a PER question, not an SOF question. The SOF is satisfied by the signed writing.
The PER bars prior agreements and contemporaneous oral ones that conflict with a final writing.

Correct. Under § 2-202(b), consistent additional terms may supplement a final writing unless the court finds the writing was intended as a complete and exclusive statement of the terms. The merger clause supports that finding.
topic: Shorthand · PER (§ 2-202) — PER: consistent term vs. complete and exclusive writing

q: A contract for 80 office chairs says "F.O.B. Seller's plant, Dover. Freight prepaid by Seller." Seller ships properly and gives notice. The chairs are destroyed in a warehouse fire at the carrier's hub on the way to Buyer. Buyer argues that because Seller paid the freight, Seller bore the transit risk. Is Buyer right?
o: No, because a buyer bears the risk of loss in every contract that involves a carrier.
No. A seller's agreement to pay freight doesn't make a shipment contract a destination one.
Yes. A seller who pays the freight to the buyer's door has agreed to deliver the goods there.
Yes. The freight-prepaid clause conflicts with the F.O.B. term, so the court construes it against Seller.
No, but only because the loss happened at the carrier's hub rather than on the road.
oe: Not in every contract. In a destination contract the seller keeps the risk until tender at the destination.

Correct. Comment 5 to § 2-503 says a term requiring the seller to pay the freight does not by itself make it a destination contract. F.O.B. Seller's plant is a shipment term, so risk passed on delivery to the carrier (§ 2-509(1)(a)).
Paying freight is a cost term, not an agreement to tender at the destination. The F.O.B. term controls.
The two terms don't conflict. One allocates cost, the other sets the delivery point and risk.
Where in transit the loss happens doesn't matter. Risk passed when the carrier took the chairs.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB shipment & destination (§ 2-319(1)(a), (b)) — Seller prepays freight under FOB seller's plant

q: Under a "C.I.F. Port of Baltimore" contract for 300 bicycles, the seller tenders the bill of lading, insurance certificate, and invoice while the ship is at sea. The buyer refuses to pay until it can open the crates. The contract says nothing else about payment. Which statement is correct?
o: The buyer must pay now, but only half the price until the bicycles arrive.
The buyer may refuse the documents, because C.I.F. requires delivery of the goods themselves.
The buyer may withhold payment until it inspects, because inspection always comes before payment.
The buyer must pay now, but paying doesn't stop it from rejecting nonconforming bikes later.
The buyer must pay now, and by paying it accepts the bicycles and waives any defects.
oe: Nothing in § 2-320 splits the payment. The full price is due against the documents.
Under C.I.F. the seller tenders documents. The buyer can't demand the goods in place of them (§ 2-320(4)).
That is only the default. C.I.F. and other documentary terms displace it.

Correct. Under C.I.F. the buyer must pay against tender of the documents (§ 2-320(4)), so there is no right to inspect before payment (§ 2-513(3)(b)). But payment is not acceptance and doesn't impair the right to inspect or any remedies (§ 2-512(2)).
Payment before inspection is not acceptance (§ 2-512(2)). The buyer keeps its right to reject.
topic: Shipping terms · CIF & C&F (§§ 2-320, 2-321) — CIF; buyer wants to inspect before paying

q: A contract for industrial robots says: "Any action for breach of this contract may be brought within six years after the cause of action accrues." The buyer sues five years after the breach accrued. What is the most likely result?
o: The claim is timely, because the parties are free to vary Article 2's default rules.
The claim is barred, because the parties may shorten the four years but may not extend it.
The claim is barred, because the clause makes the whole contract unconscionable.
The claim is timely, because six years is the general contract SOL in most states.
None of the above.
oe: Freedom of contract has limits (§ 1-302). Section 2-725(1) expressly forbids extending the period.
Correct. Under § 2-725(1), the parties may reduce the period of limitation to not less than one year but may not extend it. The four-year limit still applies.
The clause is simply ineffective to extend the period. Unconscionability isn't the reason.
Article 2's own four-year period governs sales of goods.
One of the other choices is correct: The claim is barred, because the parties may shorten the four years but may not extend it.
topic: Shorthand · SOL (§ 2-725) — SOL: parties can't extend it

q: A seller has 100 identified, conforming generators ready to ship to a buyer under a shipment contract. Before shipment, the buyer wrongfully repudiates. Three days later, a fire at the seller's warehouse destroys the generators, worth $200,000. The seller's insurance pays $150,000. What may the seller recover from the buyer for the loss?
o: Nothing, because the seller's insurer must cover the entire loss.
Nothing, because the risk never passed to the buyer before the fire.
$50,000, the amount the seller's insurance didn't cover.
$100,000, because the loss is split equally when a buyer is in breach.
$200,000, because the buyer's repudiation shifted the whole risk to the buyer.
oe: The insurer paid what its policy covered. Section 2-510(3) lets the seller look to the buyer for the shortfall.
Section 2-510(3) is an exception to that result for a breaching buyer.

Correct. When conforming goods are identified and the buyer repudiates before risk passes, the seller may, to the extent of any deficiency in its insurance coverage, treat the risk as resting on the buyer for a commercially reasonable time (§ 2-510(3)).
The Code doesn't split the loss. The buyer bears the uninsured portion.
The shift is only to the extent of the seller's insurance deficiency. The insurer covers the rest.
topic: Shipping terms · No term, presumptions & breach (§§ 2-503, 2-509, 2-510) — Buyer repudiates; seller's insurance shortfall

q: Which of the following is the best example of a course of performance?
o: The buyer's purchasing manager always intended to insist on strict delivery dates.
Under this contract, the buyer keeps accepting Friday deliveries without objecting.
Once, under this contract, the buyer accepted a delivery that arrived a day late.
Everyone in the regional produce trade lets buyers return bruised fruit within 24 hours.
In five earlier contracts between the same parties, the seller always shipped by rail.
oe: Unexpressed intent isn't conduct, so it can't form a course of performance.

Correct. A course of performance is a sequence of conduct under the particular transaction, involving repeated occasions of performance that the other party knows of and accepts or acquiesces in without objection (§ 1-303(a)).
A single occasion isn't a course of performance. It requires repeated occasions.
A regular practice in a trade is a usage of trade (§ 1-303(c)).
Conduct in earlier transactions is a course of dealing (§ 1-303(b)).
topic: Shorthand · CoP, CoD & UoT (§ 1-303) — What counts as a course of performance

q: A grain cooperative has hedge-to-arrive contracts with a farmer. The market turns sharply against the farmer, he stops returning calls, and the state attorney general announces that some HTA contracts may be illegal. The coop sends a written demand for adequate assurance, asking for a written promise to deliver and some security. The farmer doesn't respond for 45 days. What is the result?
o: The farmer has repudiated by failing to give adequate assurance within 30 days.
Nothing yet. Silence is not a repudiation until the delivery date passes without delivery.
The coop breached by making a demand, because only the farmer's own conduct can create insecurity.
The coop must wait a reasonable time, which in farming is at least 90 days.
The farmer is excused, because the attorney general's statement made the contracts illegal.
oe: Correct. The coop had reasonable grounds for insecurity, which can come from market conditions and public statements (§ 2-609(1), (2)). Failure to provide adequate assurance within a reasonable time, not over 30 days, after a justified demand is a repudiation (§ 2-609(4)). See Top of Iowa Coop. v. Sime Farms.
After a justified demand, silence for more than 30 days is a repudiation under § 2-609(4).
Insecurity can arise from market conditions and public statements, not just the other party's conduct.
Section 2-609(4) caps the reasonable time at 30 days.
The AG said only that some HTAs might be illegal. That fed the coop's insecurity; it didn't excuse the farmer.
topic: Shorthand · HTA, LOC & PDM (§ 2-609) — HTA: silence after a justified demand

q: Under a "no arrival, no sale" contract for 2,000 sacks of coffee, the ship arrives, but seawater has ruined 500 of the sacks through no fault of either party. What may the buyer do?
o: Treat the contract as avoided only if more than half the sacks were ruined.
Nothing. It must take all 2,000 sacks and pay the full price.
Reject the ruined sacks and demand that the seller ship replacements.
Treat the contract as avoided, or accept the rest at a reduced price.
Sue the seller for damages on the 500 ruined sacks.
oe: There is no 50% threshold. Any partial loss gives the buyer the § 2-613 options.
Section 2-324(b) gives the buyer the § 2-613 options.
Under § 2-324 the seller has no duty to replace goods lost or damaged without its fault.

Correct. Under § 2-324(b), when the goods arrive partly lost or deteriorated, the buyer may proceed as if there had been casualty to identified goods (§ 2-613): demand inspection and either treat the contract as avoided or accept the goods with due allowance from the price.
The seller didn't promise arrival in good condition, so there is no breach and no damages.
topic: Shipping terms · Ex-ship & no arrival, no sale (§§ 2-322, 2-324) — No arrival, no sale; partial deterioration

q: Which of the following statements about risk of loss under Article 2 is NOT correct?
o: A nonconforming tender that gives a right of rejection keeps the risk on the seller.
A merchant seller that delivers directly keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods.
The parties may allocate the risk of loss differently by agreement.
If the contract is silent, a contract to ship goods is presumed to be a shipment contract.
Risk of loss passes to the buyer when title to the goods passes.
oe: This is correct (§ 2-510(1)). The risk stays on the seller until cure or acceptance.
This is correct (§ 2-509(3)).
This is correct (§ 2-509(4)).
This is correct (§ 2-503 cmt. 5).
Correct. This statement is wrong, which makes it the answer. Article 2 deliberately separates risk from title. Risk depends on the manner of tender and whether the tender conforms (§ 2-509; § 2-401).
topic: Shipping terms · No term, presumptions & breach (§§ 2-503, 2-509, 2-510) — NOT a correct risk-of-loss statement

q: A seller agrees to sell 500 crates of machine parts "F.O.B. vessel, Port of Baltimore, to be named by Buyer." The shipping date passes and Buyer never names a vessel, despite Seller's requests. What can Seller do?
o: Treat it as a failure of cooperation under § 2-311.
Sue immediately for the price under § 2-709, because the goods are identified.
Pick any vessel sailing for the buyer's region, after which Buyer bears all the risk.
Nothing, because Seller's duty to load is absolute and it bears the risk of any delay.
Convert the contract to F.A.S. and deliver the crates alongside any ship at the port.
oe: Correct. Under F.O.B. vessel the buyer must name the vessel (§ 2-319(1)(c)) and seasonably give instructions (§ 2-319(3)). Failure is a failure of cooperation under § 2-311: Seller is excused for the resulting delay and may proceed in any reasonable manner, or treat it as a breach.
An action for the price requires accepted goods, goods lost after risk passed, or goods the seller can't resell. None applies yet.
The statute doesn't let the seller name the vessel for the buyer. It offers the § 2-311 remedies instead.
Seller's duty depends on Buyer's cooperation. Section 2-311 protects Seller when that cooperation isn't given.
Nothing in the Code lets one party change the delivery term on its own.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB vessel & FAS (§ 2-319(1)(c), (2) to (4)) — Buyer fails to name the vessel

q: A purchase order reads: "500 cases of canned tomatoes. Price: $18 per case F.O.B. Buyer's store, Newark, Delaware." Nothing else in the contract mentions delivery. The cases are lost when the carrier's truck overturns. Seller argues the F.O.B. language was only a pricing term. Who bears the loss?
o: Buyer, because the purchase order was the buyer's own form and is construed against it.
Neither party, because the contract is too indefinite to enforce without a delivery term.
Seller, because an F.O.B. term is a delivery term even when used only with the stated price.
Seller, but only if Buyer can show the parties discussed delivery before signing.
Buyer, because a term attached only to the price says nothing about who bears the risk.
oe: Nothing needs construing. The statute gives the F.O.B. term its meaning.
Even with no delivery term the contract wouldn't fail; gap fillers supply one. And here there is a delivery term.

Correct. Under § 2-319(1), unless otherwise agreed, F.O.B. is a delivery term "even though used only in connection with the stated price." F.O.B. Buyer's store is a destination term, so risk stayed with Seller until tender at Newark.
No extrinsic evidence is needed. The statute makes the F.O.B. language a delivery term.
Section 2-319(1) rejects that reading. The F.O.B. term is a delivery term wherever it appears.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB shipment & destination (§ 2-319(1)(a), (b)) — FOB term used only with the price

q: A seller ships cocoa "C.I.F. Port of Wilmington, price per pound based on net landed weights." When the seller tenders the documents, the cocoa is still at sea. The buyer says it owes nothing until the cocoa is weighed on arrival. What does the buyer owe now?
o: Only the freight and insurance charges, with the cost of the cocoa due on arrival.
The full price based on the shipped weight, with no later adjustment.
Nothing until the cocoa lands and is weighed, because the price can't be known until then.
A reasonable estimate of the price, paid against the documents, adjusted after weighing.
Nothing at all, because a price based on arrival weights makes the contract too indefinite.
oe: The C.I.F. price is a lump sum. The estimated full price is due against the documents.
The contract bases the price on landed weights, so the estimate is adjusted after arrival.
Section 2-321(1) solves that problem with a reasonable estimate. Payment against documents is still due.

Correct. Under § 2-321(1), when a C.I.F. price is based on arrival weights, the seller must reasonably estimate the price, the amount due on the documents is that estimate, and the price is settled after final adjustment.
An open price doesn't defeat the contract, and § 2-321(1) supplies the method.
topic: Shipping terms · CIF & C&F (§§ 2-320, 2-321) — CIF; price based on arrival weights

q: A contract for 200 cartons of printer paper says "F.O.B. Buyer's loading dock, Newark." The carrier arrives at 2 a.m. on a Sunday, when Buyer is closed and nobody has been told to expect a delivery. The driver leaves the pallets on the dock. By morning they have been stolen. Who bears the loss?
o: Buyer, because the goods physically reached the destination named in the F.O.B. term.
Seller, because goods left at a closed dock at 2 a.m. weren't duly tendered.
Buyer, because it would have received the goods had it been open for business.
The carrier, because the driver chose to leave the pallets without a signature.
Buyer, because a buyer must keep its dock secure for any deliveries that may arrive.
oe: Arrival isn't enough. The goods must be duly tendered, at a reasonable hour and with notice.

Correct. Risk passes in a destination contract only on due tender at the destination (§ 2-509(1)(b)). Tender must be at a reasonable hour, with any notice reasonably needed to let the buyer take delivery (§ 2-503(1)).
Due tender requires a reasonable hour. A 2 a.m. Sunday drop with no notice doesn't qualify.
The carrier may be liable to Seller, but as between Seller and Buyer the risk never passed.
The burden is on the seller to make a proper tender. The buyer wasn't told to expect this delivery.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB shipment & destination (§ 2-319(1)(a), (b)) — FOB destination; tender at an unreasonable hour

q: A buyer emails a seller: "We'll take 2,000 units of part 44-B at $3.10 each. Thanks, Dana Reyes, Purchasing." The buyer later refuses the goods and argues the SOF isn't satisfied because nobody signed anything on paper. Is the buyer right?
o: Yes. The SOF requires a handwritten signature on a paper writing.
Yes. A signature block in an email is just a habit, not an intent to sign.
No, but only because the seller is a merchant and can rely on § 2-201(2).
Yes. An email can satisfy the SOF only if it carries a certified digital signature.
No. A typed name in an email, adopted to authenticate the record, is a signature.
oe: Both the UCC and UETA treat electronic records and signatures as satisfying writing and signature rules.
Courts generally treat a typed name at the end of a business email as adopting it, and the outline flags this as almost certainly a signature.
The buyer's own email is signed by the party to be charged, so § 2-201(1) is satisfied directly.
No special technology is required. Intent to adopt the record is what counts.

Correct. "Sign" includes attaching or associating an electronic symbol with intent to adopt or accept a record (§ 1-201(b)(37), 2022 amendments), and UETA § 7 gives the same result in states without those amendments. The email states a quantity and indicates a contract, so § 2-201(1) is satisfied.
topic: Shorthand · UETA & e-signatures — UETA: typed name in an email

q: A contract for 20 commercial freezers says "F.O.B. Seller's warehouse, C.O.D." Seller ships properly and gives notice. The freezers are destroyed when the carrier's truck catches fire. The buyer argues that because it was to pay on delivery, the seller kept the risk until payment. Who bears the loss?
o: The seller, because C.O.D. turns any shipment contract into a destination contract.
The seller, because it retained a security interest in the freezers until payment.
The buyer, because C.O.D. is only a payment term.
The seller, because a seller who ships C.O.D. keeps the risk until it is paid.
The buyer, but only if it had already paid part of the price in advance.
oe: Nothing in the Code gives C.O.D. that effect. It is a payment term.
A shipment under reservation doesn't change the risk rule (§ 2-509(1)(a)).

Correct. C.O.D. only governs when payment is due and whether the buyer may inspect first (§ 2-513(3)(a)). The risk is set by the delivery term, and F.O.B. Seller's warehouse passed it on delivery to the carrier (§ 2-509(1)(a)).
Risk doesn't follow payment, just as it doesn't follow title. The F.O.B. term controls.
Prior payment has nothing to do with it. The risk passed under the F.O.B. term.
topic: Shipping terms · COD & payment against documents (§§ 2-512, 2-513) — COD is not a risk term

q: A fully integrated written contract for "500 tons of coal" contains a merger clause. The seller offers evidence that in the coal trade in that region, "ton" means a long ton of 2,240 pounds. The buyer objects that the merger clause bars all outside evidence. Is the seller's evidence admissible?
o: Yes. Trade usage may explain or supplement even a complete and exclusive writing.
Yes, but only if the buyer is also a member of the coal trade.
No, because usage of trade must be proved by a written trade code.
No. Usage of trade can only be used when the writing is ambiguous on its face.
No. A merger clause bars every kind of extrinsic evidence.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-202(a), terms in a final writing may be explained or supplemented by course of performance, course of dealing, or usage of trade. The complete-and-exclusive limit in § 2-202(b) applies only to consistent additional terms.
A usage binds parties who are or should be aware of it (§ 1-303(c)). Membership isn't the test.
Usage of trade is proved as a fact. A written code is only one way to prove it.
Article 2 doesn't require a finding of ambiguity first (§ 2-202 cmt. 1(c)).
A merger clause bears on § 2-202(b). It doesn't shut out the CoP, CoD, and UoT evidence that § 2-202(a) admits.
topic: Shorthand · PER (§ 2-202) — PER: usage of trade explains a complete writing

q: A buyer contracts for steel coils "F.O.B. vessel M/V Liberty, Port of Wilmington" and names the Liberty as required. To save time, the seller loads the coils onto the M/V Harmony, which sails first, and sends the buyer the bill of lading. The Harmony sinks. Who bears the loss?
o: The buyer, because the coils were loaded on board a vessel and the risk passed on loading.
The seller, but only if the buyer can prove the Liberty would not have sunk.
The buyer, because the Harmony sailed sooner and the change benefited the buyer.
The buyer, because it accepted the bill of lading the seller sent.
The seller, because it never loaded the coils on board the vessel the contract named.
oe: Risk passes on loading on the vessel the contract names. A different ship isn't performance.
No causation showing is needed. The tender didn't conform, so the risk never passed.
A seller can't substitute performance just because it thinks the change helps the buyer.
Receiving a document isn't acceptance of the goods, and the defect wasn't one the buyer had a chance to waive.
Correct. F.O.B. vessel requires the seller to load the goods on board the named vessel (§ 2-319(1)(c)). Loading a different ship isn't a conforming tender, so § 2-510(1) keeps the risk on the seller.
topic: Shipping terms · FOB vessel & FAS (§ 2-319(1)(c), (2) to (4)) — FOB vessel; seller loads the wrong ship
